entries.answer:
Here’s a secure, practical onboarding checklist you can use for Anthropic API access.

### 1) Create the Anthropic Console account

Go to `console.anthropic.com` and sign up with a work-controlled email address if possible. Use a strong, unique password and enable any available multi-factor authentication on the account if Anthropic offers it in your region or plan. Keep the account tied to the team or project that will actually use the API, because access should be easy to revoke if roles change.

### 2) Verify the email address

After registration, confirm the verification email before doing anything else. This step matters because unverified accounts can delay approval and create confusion later if password resets, billing notices, or policy emails never reach you. If the email does not arrive quickly, check spam and allowlist-related filtering before requesting another link.

### 3) Write a clear use-case description

Anthropic may ask what you plan to build, so prepare a short, honest description of the intended application. Include the product name, the type of users, the main tasks Claude will perform, and whether the system is internal, customer-facing, or experimental. A good description makes approval smoother because it shows that you understand the intended usage and are not hiding anything unusual.

### 4) Set up billing

Add a valid payment method in the console and confirm the billing profile details are correct. If your organization uses purchase orders or a shared corporate card, make sure the finance owner understands API usage can scale quickly depending on request volume and model choice. Set internal spend limits or monitoring alerts if your organization supports them, so billing surprises are less likely.

### 5) Understand approval timing

Approval times can vary depending on account verification, use-case review, billing setup, and current platform load. In practice, some accounts are enabled quickly, while others may need manual review and take longer. Plan for a delay and avoid building a launch-critical dependency until the account is confirmed active.

### 6) Create the API key

Once access is enabled, generate an API key in the console for the specific project or environment you need. Treat this key like a password: anyone who has it can potentially use your API quota. Prefer separate keys for development, staging, and production so you can revoke one environment without breaking everything else.

### 7) Make the first Claude API test request

Before integrating deeply, do one minimal test request from a local machine or controlled test environment. For example, verify the key works by sending a simple message request to Claude and confirming you receive a valid response. Keep this test isolated so you can debug authentication, network, and model-selection issues without exposing the key broadly.

### 8) Store `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` safely

Store the key in an environment variable rather than hardcoding it into source files. For local development, set it in your shell session or a local `.env` file that is excluded from version control. In production, use a secret manager or your platform’s managed environment-variable mechanism, and restrict access so only the running service can read it. For example, your application can read `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment at runtime, while the secret itself never appears in the repository.

### 9) Rotate immediately after exposure

If the key is ever exposed, assume it is compromised and rotate it right away. Create a new key, update every active deployment and automation job, then revoke the old one once you confirm the new key is working. Rotation should also happen on a regular schedule, even if no incident occurred, because periodic refresh reduces the damage if a secret was copied somewhere unnoticed.

### 10) Audit where the key may have spread

Check source code, configuration files, shell history, CI/CD logs, build logs, issue trackers, pasted chat messages, screenshots, and any tickets where someone may have pasted the token. Search your git history too, because deleting a line from the current branch does not remove it from past commits. If your team uses chat tools or AI assistants, review those conversations as well, since people often paste secrets there during debugging.

### 11) Clean up and prevent repeat leaks

After an incident, remove the secret from every place you find it, not just the most obvious one. Revoke old credentials, invalidate cached builds if needed, and update documentation to show the correct secret-handling process. Then add safeguards such as secret scanning, pre-commit hooks, `.gitignore` rules for local env files, and an internal rule that no one shares API keys in chat or tickets.

### 12) Good first-practice checklist

Use a separate development key, keep billing visible to the right owner, and verify that the first request succeeds before scaling up. Log only non-sensitive request metadata, never the secret itself. When in doubt, assume any copied key is public and rotate it.

If you want, I can turn this into a one-page internal SOP or a copy-paste checklist for your engineering team.
